messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric transducer (current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$).
    *   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ via storage capacitor $C_{out}$ at node "out".
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean).
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (absolute max).
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (at the end).
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (cold start to $1.8\text{ V}$).
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability).
    *   Conditions (S1-S6): Varying loads ($150\text{ k}\Omega$ to $2200\text{ k}\Omega$), excitation currents ($30\text{ }\mu\text{A}$ to $100\text{ }\mu\text{A}$), and frequencies.

    *   Reference FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier):
        *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{ V}$ (FAIL, too low).
        *   S3 (strong excitation, light load): $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$ (FAIL, too high).
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{ V}$ (FAIL, too low).
    *   Key Problems:
        1.  Low output voltage for weak/heavy loads (diode drops, poor impedance matching).
        2.  Overvoltage for strong/light loads (lack of regulation/clamping).

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):*
        *   Increases harvested energy by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, reducing the effective capacitance and increasing the voltage swing.
        *   Structure: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Storage, with an L-S switch to invert $C_p$.
    *   *Synchronous Rectification:*
        *   Replacing diodes with switches to eliminate diode drops.
    *   *Zener Clamping:*
        *   To prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding $3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI-based (Half-bridge or Full-bridge).*
        *   Since we have limited components (16), let's try a simple SSHI.
        *   Standard SSHI uses a rectifier and an inductor switch to invert the piezo voltage.
        *   Let's use a full-bridge rectifier for efficiency and a Zener for clamping.
        *   To invert $C_p$, we need an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ across the piezo terminals (pzp, pzn).
        *   Sync controller $G1$ closes $S$ at peaks (both edges). $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.

    *   *Design 2: Improved Full Bridge with Zener and larger storage.*
        *   Standard FBR but with a Zener clamp to handle S3.
        *   (Wait, the goal is to solve S2 and S4 too. FBR isn't enough for S2/S4).

    *   *Design 3: SSHI with a more aggressive voltage boost.*
        *   Instead of just a rectifier, maybe a switch-capacitor or inductor-based boost?
        *   Actually, let's stick to a known efficient topology: SSHI with a bridge.

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor)**
        *   Full bridge (DSCH) $\to$ storage $C_{out} \to$ load $R_L$.
        *   Inductor $L_1$ and switch $S_1$ across pzp-pzn.
        *   $S_1$ closes at peaks to flip $C_p$ voltage.
        *   Zener $D_{z}$ on "out" to prevent overvoltage.
        *   Components: 4 Diodes (bridge), 1 Zener, 1 Inductor, 1 Switch, 1 Sync, 1 Capacitor. (Total 9 components).

    *   **Proposal 2: SSHI with a simpler rectifier (Half-bridge)**
        *   If $pzn$ is tied to ground (or via diode), we might save components, but FBR is usually better for sinusoidal sources.
        *   Let's try a different SSHI variant: Parallel-SSHI.
        *   Actually, a better "second attempt" is often a variant of the first or a completely different approach like a Charge Pump, but with $100\text{ Hz}$ and low voltage, SSHI is the gold standard.

    *   **Proposal 3: Synchronous Rectifier (If possible)**
        *   The "S" switch is limited to 4. A full synchronous rectifier would take 4 switches.
        *   But we only have 2 SYNC controllers.
        *   Maybe a switch-based rectifier? No, let's try a "Zener-Clamped FBR" as a baseline, but the prompt says FBR failed S2 and S4. We need more *voltage*.

    *   *Wait, let's refine the SSHI.*
        The core of SSHI is to flip the voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$.
        The circuit:
        1.  Rectifier: $D_1$ [pzp, out], $D_2$ [pzn, out], $D_3$ [0, pzp], $D_4$ [0, pzn].
        2.  Zener: $D_z$ [0, out] (cathode on out).
        3.  Inverter: $L_1$ [pzp, n1], $S_1$ [n1, pzn].
        4.  Controller: $G_1$ (edges: both, phase: 0).
        5.  Storage: $C_1$ [out, 0].

    *   *Wait, the Reference FBR failed S2 ($1.76\text{ V}$) and S4 ($1.51\text{ V}$).*
        SSHI significantly increases the voltage across the rectifier.
        $V_{peak\_rect} \approx V_{oc} \cdot \frac{1}{1-\gamma}$, where $\gamma$ is the reflection coefficient. This should push S2 and S4 above $1.8\text{ V}$.
        S3 ($V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$) is fixed by the Zener.

    *   Let's check component counts:
        D1-D4 (Bridge), Dz (Zener), L1, S1, G1, C1. Total = 9. Well within 16.

    *   *Is there a better way to invert?*
        Some SSHI designs use a switch directly across pzp-pzn.
        $L_1$ [pzp, n1], $S_1$ [n1, pzn] is effectively a switch in series with an inductor. This is correct.

    *   *Let's try a different topology for Proposal 2: "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI).*
        P-SSHI uses an additional capacitor to store the flipped charge.
        But that's more complex. Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" approach using the limited switches.
        Wait, I can't do a full synchronous rectifier with 2 SYNCs and 4 switches effectively without complex timing.

    *   *What about Proposal 2 as a "Boost" circuit?*
        A piezo is a current source. An inductor-based boost (like a DC-DC) needs a way to rectify first.
        Actually, a "Synchronized Switch" can be applied to the rectifier itself (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction - SECE).
        SECE topology:
        Piezo $\to$ $C_{fly}$ (via switch $S_1$) $\to$ rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        This is often more efficient than SSHI.
        SECE components:
        - Switch $S_1$ from pzp to $C_{fly}$ node.
        - $C_{fly}$ from node to 0.
        - Diode $D_1$ from $C_{fly}$ to out.
        - Switch $S_2$ from pzn to 0 (to clamp piezo during extraction).
        - $G_1$ for $S_1$, $G_2$ for $S_2$.
        Wait, SECE requires specific timing. Let's stick to SSHI first.

    *   *Proposal 2: FBR with Zener (Basic check)*
        Even if FBR failed, maybe with a different $C_{out}$ and Zener it's a stable baseline? No, the prompt says it failed S2/S4, and the evolution strategy will optimize $C_{out}$. The topology is the problem.

    *   *Proposal 3: SSHI with different Switch Configuration.*
        Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge (one diode to out, one diode to ground) if we can bias the piezo. But the piezo is a current source, so it needs a return path.

    *   *Let's refine Proposal 1 (SSHI) and Proposal 2 (SECE).*

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor)**
        - D1: pzp -> out
        - D2: pzn -> out
        - D3: 0 -> pzp
        - D4: 0 -> pzn
        - Dz: 0 -> out (Zener)
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn
        - G1: Sync (both edges, ton ~ 30us)
        - C1: out -> 0

    *   **Proposal 2: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)**
        - S1: pzp -> n_fly (ctrl: G1, edges: pos)
        - C_fly: n_fly -> 0
        - D1: n_fly -> out
        - S2: pzn -> 0 (ctrl: G2, edges: pos) - *Wait, SECE typically flips the piezo to a reference.*
        Actually, a simpler SECE:
        S1 [pzp, n_fly], C_fly [n_fly, 0], D1 [n_fly, out], S2 [pzn, 0].
        G1: edges="pos", G2: edges="pos".
        Wait, a more standard SECE is:
        S1 [pzp, n_fly] (closes at peak)
        D1 [n_fly, out]
        C_fly [n_fly, 0]
        S2 [pzn, 0] (closes at peak)
        And then for the negative peak:
        S3 [pzn, n_fly] (closes at peak)
        S4 [pzp, 0] (closes at peak)
        This uses 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.

    *   *Let's rethink the SECE with 2 SYNCs:*
        G1 (edges: pos) -> S1 [pzp, n_fly], S2 [pzn, 0]
        G2 (edges: neg) -> S3 [pzn, n_fly], S4 [pzp, 0]
        This is the classic SECE. Let's check components: 4 S, 2 SYNC, 1 C_fly, 1 D1, 1 C_out. Total = 9.

    *   **Proposal 3: SSHI with "Half-Bridge" (Efficiency check)**
        Let's try an SSHI but with a more optimized rectifier if possible. Actually, just try the SSHI with a Zener and different storage.
        Wait, let's try a "Voltage Doubler" (Dickson) style? No, too many diode drops.

    *   S2/S4 failure: Low $V_{out}$. SSHI and SECE both increase the voltage.
    *   S3 failure: High $V_{out}$. Zener clamp is necessary.
    *   Ripple/Settled: Large $C_{out}$ and proper $t_{on}$ will help.

    *Refining Proposal 1 (SSHI):*
    - D1 [pzp, out]
    - D2 [pzn, out]
    - D3 [0, pzp]
    - D4 [0, pzn]
    - Dz [0, out] (Zener)
    - L1 [pzp, n1]
    - S1 [n1, pzn]
    - G1 [SYNC]
    - C1 [out, 0]

    *Refining Proposal 2 (SECE):*
    - S1 [pzp, n_fly] (G1, pos)
    - S2 [pzn, 0] (G1, pos)
    - S3 [pzn, n_fly] (G2, neg)
    - S4 [pzp, 0] (G2, neg)
    - C_fly [n_fly, 0]
    - D1 [n_fly, out]
    - Dz [0, out] (Zener)
    - C1 [out, 0]
    - G1 [SYNC, pos]
    - G2 [SYNC, neg]

    *Refining Proposal 3 (Modified FBR with Zener):*
    Wait, FBR was already tested. Let's try a different approach for Proposal 3:
    A "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI) is essentially SSHI but the inductor is not across the piezo, but instead used to transfer charge to a separate capacitor before it goes to the output.
    Or, just try a simple "Boost" using one of the SYNCs.
    Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" to see if it helps.
    Actually, a very simple and effective one is the "inductor-based boost" where you rectify first, then use a SYNC switch to boost $V_{out}$.
    Rectifier $\to C_{mid} \to L \to S \to C_{out}$.
    But we have to be careful with the 16-component limit.

    Let's go with:
    1. SSHI (Full Bridge)
    2. SECE (Full)
    3. SSHI (Half Bridge) - just to see. Or maybe a "Zener-clamped FBR with a higher-order filter". No, let's try a "Cold-start optimized" SSHI.

    Actually, let's stick to the two strongest candidates: SSHI and SECE. For the third, I'll propose a "Synchronous Rectifier" attempt.
    Wait, a synchronous rectifier:
    S1 [pzp, out] (G1, pos)
    S2 [pzn, out] (G2, neg)
    S3 [0, pzp] (G2, neg)
    S4 [0, pzn] (G1, pos)
    G1 (pos), G2 (neg).
    This removes diode drops entirely! This should solve S2 and S4.
    Add a Zener to solve S3.

    *Synchronous Rectifier (SR) check:*
    - S1 [pzp, out] (G1, pos)
    - S2 [pzn, out] (G2, neg)
    - S3 [0, pzp] (G2, neg)
    - S4 [0, pzn] (G1, pos)
    - G1 [SYNC, pos], G2 [SYNC, neg]
    - Dz [0, out] (Zener)
    - C1 [out, 0]
    This is very efficient.

    *Summary of 3 Proposals:*
    1. SSHI: FBR + Inductor-Switch flip. (High voltage, good for S2/S4).
    2. SECE: Charge extraction via fly-cap. (Very high efficiency, good for S2/S4).
    3. SR: Full synchronous bridge. (Zero diode drop, good for S2/S4).

    *Wait, let's double check the SYNC controller:*
    "closes its switches for "ton" seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    For SR, $t_{on}$ needs to be half a period ($0.005\text{ s}$), but the limit is $0.001\text{ s}$.
    *CRITICAL ERROR:* The `ton` limit is $1\text{ ms}$. $100\text{ Hz}$ period is $10\text{ ms}$.
    So a SYNC switch *cannot* be used as a standard rectifier switch (which needs to be closed for $5\text{ ms}$).
    It can ONLY be used for short pulses (like in SSHI or SECE).

    *Rethink Proposal 3:*
    Since SR is impossible, let's go back to the "Half-Bridge SSHI" or "P-SSHI".
    Wait, if I can't use SYNC for rectification, I must use diodes.
    Let's try:
    1. SSHI (Full Bridge)
    2. SECE (Full)
